name: Rethink Priorities: worldview investigations and surveys (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Changes others' spending: the charities of each cause it informs, read live, bring their own countries.
summary: Rethink Priorities' worldview investigations team (cross-cause prioritisation, moral weights, digital minds, movement-building models) and its surveys team (polls and message tests for effective-giving organisations and funders); this model covers both in 2025 ($1.03M, $1.7M with their share of central costs), a branch each. With no published count of what their work changed, we judge that about $0.3M of cause-neutral funders' spending and $0.25M of organisations' spending was steered by them in the year, valued at its gain from an ordinary charity of each cause to that cause's portfolio, live, in our judgment of the teams' 2025 work (global health 25%, animal welfare 35%, AI safety 30%; digital minds and movement work drop out), after a 0.6 evidence step for contested cross-cause judgments and the missing-data discount. At the defaults that is about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, with the next dollar at 31% of the past average; the result is mostly uncertainty in our judgments of the money informed, the share changed and the cause weights (animal welfare's share is worth almost nothing at the site's animal weights, so the result follows the global health and AI shares), and both branches are discounted for missing data.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

source.page: Part III line 4a (expenses, grants, revenue); Schedule O

rows.explainer: Form 990 Part III line 4a: Apollo Research, Epoch, Global Challenges Project, Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute, Consultants for Impact, Insect Institute, Center for AI Security and Access, Vista Institute for AI Policy, Center for Wild Animal Welfare, Scaling Impact Partners, Truthful AI and others, with the Special Projects team that runs their operations. The projects' spending is theirs, paid from money restricted to them (releases of $12.4M in 2025, accounts Note 3), not a gift to Rethink Priorities; Rethink Priorities calls the programme self-financing and leaves it out of its core budget. Taken out of the cost here. Epoch AI has its own model on this site; the others have none.

rows.label: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, incubated and sponsored, 2025 (US$)

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Form 990 for 2025 (Part III and Schedule O)

rows.explainer: Form 990 Part III line 4b ('AI policy and strategy: in 2025, RP's AI work was conducted by the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy'). The accounts list it among the sponsored projects (restricted net assets $9.28M, Note 3) and it spins off as a separate organisation in 2026: its own donors' money, not Rethink Priorities' cost, so taken out here like the other sponsored projects.

rows.label: Share of management and fundraising that serves Rethink Priorities' own research departments
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The accounts don't split management and fundraising between its own departments and the sponsored projects. Its own budget table for 2025 puts 'core operations' at $1.915M (estimated expenses, which it says include 'some additional support for our Special Projects'), with the development team outside the table; $1.915M plus most of the $0.64M of fundraising is about 70% of the $3.34M of management and fundraising in the accounts. 70% (50% to 100%): the low end has the sponsored projects' fees carry half the central costs, the high end none.

rows.label: Programme expenses of Rethink Priorities' own research departments, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Programme services less the sponsored and incubated projects: animal welfare $1,404,180, global health and development $977,837, worldview investigations $718,655 and surveys and data analysis $315,442 (Form 990 Part III and Schedule O), $3.42M, the four lines the site models.

rows.label: Total expenses of its own departments, with their share of management and fundraising, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Its own research departments' programme spending and the share of central costs that serves them: about $5.75M, close to its own estimate of $5.75M for 2025 (departments and core operations, its budget table).

rows.label: Spending on worldview investigations and surveys and data analysis, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Its two cross-cause departments: one model, a branch each (Convention 4), because both inform the same cause-neutral funders and organisations.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads the share of management and fundraising that serves its own departments over them in proportion to their cost (about 1.6).

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
rows.explainer: The department's spending with its share of central costs: what a dollar for this work pays for.

rows.label: Funders' and organisations' yearly spending its worldview research informed, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: no count is published. Its 2025 outputs (the moral parliament tool's update, the digital minds estimates and consciousness model, work on prioritising under moral uncertainty, movement-building models the Centre for Effective Altruism uses for its local-group strategy) are mostly published research paid for by grants (revenue $1,750, Schedule O). Anchored on the global health model's commissioned project ($3M informed): about three decisions of that size (the Centre for Effective Altruism's groups strategy, cause-neutral funders weighing animal against human work and digital minds) plus the readers of its tools. $10M (2 to 50 million).

rows.label: Share of that spending whose allocation the worldview research changed
rows.explainer: Our judgment: published frameworks and tools change a small share of what a funder or organisation spends; anchored on a third of the 10% we give a commissioned global health project (bought for one decision), 3% (1% to 10%).

rows.label: Spending its worldview research changed (US$)
Organisations' and funders' yearly spending its surveys informed, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most of its projects are private commissions; the public ones are Open Philanthropy's surveys of how people use large language models, the second wave of its Pulse survey of US attitudes to effective and charitable giving, the effective-giving community survey and a survey of the Meta Coordination Forum's decision-makers. They inform outreach and messaging budgets of effective-giving organisations. Anchored on the global health model's commission ($3M per project), with its revenue ($38,308) showing few paid projects and most pro bono or grant-funded: about two decisions of that size, $5M (1 to 20 million).

rows.label: Share of that spending whose use its surveys changed
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a survey bought for a decision (a message, an audience, a framing) changes more of it than published research (3%) and less than a commissioned strategy report (10%, the global health model); 5% (1% to 15%).

rows.label: Spending its surveys changed (US$)
Money moved: funders' and organisations' spending whose allocation its 2025 cross-cause research and surveys changed (US$)
rows.explainer: The two departments' changed spending: all shifted money, which the funders and organisations would have spent anyway.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context: money changed per dollar of the two departments' cost.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar to the causes its cross-cause work informs (live), units of value
rows.explainer: Its cross-cause work and surveys inform cause-neutral funders and organisations in global health, animal welfare and AI safety. No split is published, so the weights are our judgments of the two teams' 2025 work by expenses (facts/meta.json rp_cross_cause_share_*: global health 25%, animal welfare 35%, AI 30%), each at its portfolio (#cause:global-health, #cause:animal-welfare and the AI area, #cause:ai); its digital minds and AI consciousness work (no cause on the site) and its effective-giving movement work drop out, valued at the average of the rest (normalization.md 2.8).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where the money its research changed went: the cause's charities on this site, live (value_destinations).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: an ordinary charity of each cause its money goes to, in its own mix), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the shared rule for an organisation whose money goes to several causes. Shifted money would have gone to an ordinary charity of the same cause: each cause's at the rule for a mover in that cause (GiveDirectly's live result, times a shared multiple, 1×, from 0 to 3×, over the global-health charities' on the rankings, times that cause's charities'), weighted by the organisation's own split, all live under your values.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: Value of a dollar all shifted (given anyway, now to a better use), at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: Money that would have been given or spent anyway counts only for the gain over where it would have gone: a grantmaker's grants, or spending that research or advice changed. Its owners spent it, so the organisation is credited its share of that gain (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the spending its research or advice changed (all shifted money), units of value
rows.explainer: Spending its research or advice changed, at a judged share of the money it informed: all of it would have been spent anyway, so it counts for the gain over where it would have gone, discounted for weak evidence and for an outcome not measured for this charity (docs/normalization.md 2.8, 2.12).

rows.label: People or animals per year the policy or research would affect
rows.explainer: 0: its research reaches people and animals through the decisions it changes, counted below as money whose allocation changed. The one policy opportunity it reports (animal welfare's rapid response to 'a confidential opportunity to influence welfare policy guidelines', report p. 31) has no published outcome, so it is in the animal welfare model's side effects, not a branch. The policy branch's rows multiply nothing.

rows.label: Value per unit affected per year, in units of value
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Expected value of the policy or research (before adjustments)
Careers changed to high-impact work in the year modelled
rows.explainer: 0: Rethink Priorities reports no career changes it caused. It trained or advised 30+ early-career researchers through fellowships and collaborations in 2025 (report p. 7), but publishes no count of where they went; they are in the side effects.

rows.label: Pay a career changer gives up per year (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's shared default (facts/meta.json) while careers_changed is 0: Rethink Priorities' research changes no careers it counts, so this multiplies nothing.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays in high-impact work
rows.explainer: The site's shared default (facts/meta.json) while careers_changed is 0: Rethink Priorities' research changes no careers it counts, so this multiplies nothing.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays, discounted
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of the new employers' work (units of value)
rows.explainer: Unused while careers_changed is 0; it reads the destinations the money goes to.

rows.label: Share of the career changes the charity caused
rows.explainer: The site's shared default (facts/meta.json) while careers_changed is 0: Rethink Priorities' research changes no careers it counts, so this multiplies nothing.

rows.label: Value of one career change (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one career-change step (docs/normalization.md 2.8), at the mobiliser's share (2.24): the person gives up the pay.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Unused: no careers changed (careers_changed is 0), so this row multiplies nothing.

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the share of the gain counted that is real. Cross-cause frameworks rest on contested moral and empirical judgments, so a changed allocation is less surely better than within one cause; 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), below its other departments' 0.7.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what the funders and organisations would have done without the research is netted out in each branch's share of the money it changed (Convention 5: one question, asked once).

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: 1: other advisers and the funders' own staff are netted out in each branch's share of the money it changed, which counts only the part its research changed.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The skeleton's policy branch, unused here (0): its share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24). The money moved and the careers take the mobiliser's share in their own rows.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (the site's missing-data step, docs/normalization.md 2.12): the money informed is its own report or our judgment and the share it changed is our judgment, with no follow-up of what the funders did differently; Rethink Priorities says it reports outputs and is building an evaluation of its downstream effects. Applied to every branch.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, applied to the money its research changed and to the empty policy branch.

rows.label: Side effects of its cross-cause research and surveys beyond the money counted, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Good and harm the branches leave out. Positive: academic papers and tools others build on, the field-shaping work on digital minds before it has funders, data on the effective-giving community that many groups use, and the early-career researchers it trained. Negative: staff time of the organisations surveyed; research that points the wrong way, false precision included, is in evidence_adj. 15% (0% to +50%), our judgment, as for its animal welfare work.

rows.label: Value of the money its research changed (units of value)
rows.explainer: The spending its research and surveys changed, all shifted, at the gain of the causes' charities over an ordinary charity of each (moved_dollar_value − prior_dollar_value, the shared rule for money all shifted), after the adjustments and with the side effects.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)
rows.explainer: The policy branch is empty; the money its research changed counts its own adjustments (moved_value), careers are 0.

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: Units of value per dollar of the department's cost, central costs included.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of cost
rows.explainer: Its own share from the audited accounts (Convention 1): salaries, payroll taxes and benefits over all expenses, {{row:staff_cost_share}}, a research organisation almost all of whose cost is its remote staff. Contractors paid as other fees for services ($1.5M) are left out.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for research and policy organisations: no published salary benchmark for its staff.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: Rethink Priorities' own figure (facts/next_dollar.json): {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} (12–72%). It reports room for $9.3M against a 2026 core budget of $7.5M, but held about 11 months of its own costs without donor restrictions at the end of 2025 (its aim is about three months) and $4.74M more restricted to its own departments, about 20 months in all; for these two teams a further dollar buys mostly more of the same work (scaling cross-cause prioritisation, digital minds, surveys for near-term decisions; report pp. 20 and 35).

rows.label: Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources on, its cost shares the outcome with its staff's forgone pay. The money its research changed is all shifted (funders' and organisations' budgets), so it adds no new money to the credit, as Open Philanthropy's money in GiveWell's model.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar you give
rows.explainer: A further dollar for this department: its past average per dollar, credited by share of resources and scaled to the next dollar.
